title: Jesse Boot's Advert for 128 Cheaper Medicines, March 1877
dek: In 1877 Jesse Boot, newly in charge of the family herbalist's shop on Goose Gate, bought the biggest advert a Nottingham paper sold and bet the shop on low prices.

story.event: Taking sole control of the Goose Gate shop and advertising branded medicines at cut prices
story.summary: In 1877 Jesse Boot, newly in sole control of the family herbalist's shop on Goose Gate, Nottingham, ran a large newspaper campaign listing 128 branded medicines at reduced prices under the slogan 'health for a shilling'. Buying in bulk and selling below other chemists' prices, he raised weekly turnover to about £100 by the autumn and drew the hostility of established chemists; he hired his first qualified pharmacist in 1884 and, worn out, considered selling the business in 1885.
paragraphs: On 12 March 1877 the Nottingham Daily Express carried the largest advertisement it sold, bought by a shop on Goose Gate and filled with an alphabetical list of 128 branded medicines, each at a reduced price. The man paying was Jesse Boot, who had left school at thirteen to help his widowed mother and who had, that year, taken sole control of the family business.

His father, John, had opened the shop in 1849, selling herbal remedies to Nottingham's industrial poor. After John died in 1860, Mary Boot kept it going with ten-year-old Jesse gathering and preparing herbs, and around 1870 mother and son became partners as M & J Boot, Herbalists. Working people were turning from herbs to branded patent remedies, and in 1874 Jesse began selling them too. His idea, as he recalled it in 1904, was that a large future lay in selling them for less than the ordinary chemists charged: buy in bulk from wholesalers and sell well below the town's prices.

It was not easy at first. Wholesalers were reluctant to supply such quantities, he struggled to find the money to pay them, and he leaned on the backing of a group of Nottingham businessmen and professional men. He sold for cash, not on credit. The 1877 campaign, run under the slogan "health for a shilling", was the bet that the plan would work at scale. The university archive that holds the newspaper says profits doubled within a month. By the autumn, according to the business historian Judy Slinn, weekly turnover had reached £100, against the £20 a week he had first aimed for.

Success brought enemies. Nottingham's established chemists attacked his prices and questioned some of the goods he sold. Boot carried on. He incorporated the business in 1883 but kept control himself, and in 1884 he hired his first qualified pharmacist, Edwin Waring, who soon halved the price of prescriptions, and opened branches in Sheffield and Lincoln. In 1885, worn out, he thought about selling the whole business. He went to Jersey to rest instead.

quote.text: if the physician and the cook had to enter into a competition in which children were the judges, or men who had no more sense than children, as to which of them best understands the goodness or badness of food, the physician would be starved to death.
quote.locator: Stephanus 464d-e, Socrates to Gorgias and Polus
quote.source_title: Gorgias, tr. Benjamin Jowett, Project Gutenberg eBook #1672
quote.connection: Socrates feared that a contest judged by untrained buyers would reward whoever pleased them, not whoever knew best. Boot staked his shop on ordinary customers choosing by price, and his rivals argued much as Socrates did. Hiring a pharmacist answered part of that charge; the story does not settle the rest.

reflection: You know both sides of this. Your training trusts the person who can explain why a result is right; the people who pay for care often judge by what they can see, which is the price and the wait. Boot bet on the second group, and seven years later put a qualified pharmacist behind his counter, as if granting part of Socrates' point.

The last line of the story matters too. The man who made medicine cheaper for a whole town was, by 1885, ready to sell up because he was exhausted. Rest was not a detour from what he was building. It was what let him keep building it.
invitation: Think of one thing you offer that people mostly judge by its price. Write one sentence on the quality in it they cannot see, and one on how you could let them see it.

research_notes: Outcome figures differ in kind rather than size. The University of Nottingham's 2016 display note on the 12 March 1877 advert says profits doubled within a month; Spartacus Educational says takings doubled within a month. The story attributes 'profits doubled' to the university archive, which holds the newspaper. The £100-a-week figure is turnover (Judy Slinn, International Directory of Company Histories) or takings (Boots plc's account as quoted by Picture Nottingham), reached by the autumn of 1877 against Boot's own original target of £20 (Slinn only); the story gives it as weekly turnover and attributes it to Slinn. Dates: Boots Heritage dates the M & J Boot partnership to 1870 and Grace's Guide to about 1871, so the story says 'around 1870'. King's Lynn History says Boot began a weekly series of advertisements listing 128 items in February 1871; the university archive, which holds the paper, dates the 128-item advert to 1877, and the story follows the archive. The Boots newsroom implies he leased the larger 16-20 Goose Gate premises in 1877, while Grace's Guide and Picture Nottingham give 1881; the story leaves the move out. Slinn says the support of Nottingham businessmen and professional men helped him over his early difficulties but does not say it was equity, so funding is recorded as bootstrapped (family business, incorporated in 1883 with Boot keeping control). His 1904 recollection is reported only in Slinn's paraphrase, so the story paraphrases it without quotation marks. The 1885 health crisis: Slinn says his health declined in 1885 and he briefly considered selling; King's Lynn History says he had a breakdown in 1885, contemplated selling and took a holiday in Jersey; history.je (https://history.je/jesse-boot-of-boots-chemist-dies-in-jersey) says he went to Jersey for rest after illness brought on by overwork. Slate arc was founding-decision; the episode is the family herbalist's turn to cut-price branded medicines, so arc is change-of-direction. The Gorgias passage is Socrates' description of cookery as a flattery of medicine (Stephanus 464d-e); the Project Gutenberg Jowett text carries no Stephanus numbers or edition year. It is applied by analogy to a market that judges medicines by price.
